name: Submalar filler

card.summary: Filler injected below the cheekbone to add lower-midface volume; temporary, with only small registered trials.
card.note: Fillers are eventually resorbed; asymmetry is a listed risk.

quick.overview:
Submalar filler adds volume to the hollow beneath the cheekbones, aiming for a more defined or fuller lower midface. It is injected by clinicians, typically using hyaluronic acid.
There is general information on cheek augmentation and a few small registered trials, but little outcome data specific to this area.
quick.mechanism: A gel filler is injected into the tissue below the cheekbone, adding volume until the body gradually resorbs it.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting among risks of cheek augmentation. Filler is eventually resorbed, so results are temporary.

lead: Submalar filler is a gel dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid, injected in the hollow below the cheekbone to add volume to the lower midface. People use it to get a fuller, more lifted-looking cheek, soften a gaunt or sunken look beneath the cheekbones and create a smoother transition from cheek to jaw without surgery.[1][2]

It is the injectable counterpart of the submalar implant. Wikipedia describes submalar implants as sitting below rather than on the cheekbones, augmenting the midface especially for a gaunt or sunken look, whereas malar implants sit on the cheekbones for a higher contour.[1] Fillers are less invasive and less expensive than implants, but they are eventually resorbed, with fat described as more permanent.[1]

Dermal fillers in general last for about six months according to Wikipedia, depending on filler type, skin health, provider skill and activity in the area [2]. In the United States the FDA regulates them as medical-device implants and lists cheek volume augmentation among the approved uses of absorbable fillers for adults 22 and older [5]. Registered clinical trials of mid-face volume fillers are under way or completed [3][4].

chain: Inject gel filler below the cheekbone
Adds volume to the lower midface
angle.text: A clinician places filler in the hollow beneath the cheekbones to restore or add volume, so the lower midface looks fuller and the cheek contour more defined. The change is visible immediately and fades as the filler is resorbed.

infobox: Eventually resorbed; about six months for many fillers[1][2]
FDA-regulated medical device; cheek volume augmentation among approved uses of absorbable fillers [5]
Typically bruising, swelling and tenderness; see risks [2][5]

paras: Wikipedia describes cheek augmentation as done with implants (silicone, porous polyethylene or ePTFE) or with injectables, and distinguishes malar implants (cheekbones), submalar implants (midface) and combined implants. Fillers are injected rather than implanted, and fat, although described as more permanent, is still resorbed.[1]

Dermal filler types include hyaluronic acid, most commonly cross-linked with BDDE for stability, other natural polymers such as collagen, and synthetic polymers. Fillers are used for wrinkles and folds, age-related volume loss and contours of the lips, cheeks and jawline.[2]

The submalar area is the soft hollow beneath the cheekbone, between the cheek and the jaw. Wikipedia's cheek-augmentation article describes submalar implants as intended to augment the midface, especially for a gaunt or sunken look, in contrast with malar implants placed on the cheekbones for a higher contour [1]. Filler in the same region is used for a similar goal: adding soft-tissue volume so the lower midface looks fuller and the cheek-to-jaw transition looks smoother. Cheek and mid-face volume deficit is also the stated target of registered filler trials [3][4]. In practice, clinicians may combine cheek treatment with other areas; Wikipedia notes cheek augmentation is often combined with a face lift or chin augmentation [1].

Hyaluronic acid products such as Restylane and Juvederm are named in Wikipedia as filler options for cheek augmentation, with autologous fat described as more permanent though still eventually resorbed [1]. The dermal filler article describes hyaluronic acid fillers as most commonly cross-linked with BDDE for stability [2]. Treatment is done by injection by a clinician, in contrast with implants, which Wikipedia says are placed through an incision, usually inside the mouth, in a one- to two-hour procedure under sedation or general anaesthesia with recovery of about ten days [1].

Wikipedia states the effect of dermal fillers lasts about six months and some people need more than one injection, with duration depending on skin health, provider skill, filler type and activity in the injected area; exercise and manual labor can shorten it.[2]

The FDA regulates dermal fillers as medical-device implants and says results vary with tissue structure, the amount and type of filler and the injection site; some fillers are absorbed over time so repeat treatments may be needed [5]. It lists volume augmentation of the cheeks among approved uses of absorbable fillers in adults 22 and over, and says non-absorbable fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars [5]. The agency states that injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic use and that no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use, and it advises against self-injection or buying fillers online because products may be counterfeit or unapproved [5].
For cheek augmentation, Wikipedia lists asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting as a risk, and temporary loss of sensation as common with implants.[1]

For dermal fillers, common effects are bruising, redness, pain and itching; less commonly infections and allergic reactions that can cause lumps or scarring. Rare serious complications include blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries, and delayed skin necrosis, with embolic complications more frequent with autologous fat, followed by hyaluronic acid.[2]

The FDA identifies accidental injection into a blood vessel as the most serious concern, with possible tissue death, vision problems including blindness, and stroke that can be permanent. It lists bruising, redness, swelling, pain, tenderness, itching and rash as common, nodules, infection and allergic reactions as less common, and reports of anaphylaxis, filler migration, permanent hard nodules and death as rare; it notes that removing filler can be difficult or impossible, especially for permanent and non-hyaluronic acid products [5]. The agency advises choosing a licensed provider with dermatology or plastic-surgery experience trained in filler injection [5].

A registered study of a hyaluronic acid product for restoration of mid-face volume deficit in 30 participants began recruiting in January 2025.[3] A small completed study of the tissue filler SMI-01 in the nasolabial fold and cheek augmentation enrolled 21 participants and started in November 2020.[4] Results are not summarised in the registry entries.

timeline.event: Study of SMI-01 tissue filler for nasolabial fold and cheek augmentation begins (n=21).[4]
Study of a hyaluronic acid product for mid-face volume deficit begins recruiting (n=30).[3]
